sentences.text: I built a system that answers questions about five hundred AI interviews, entirely on my laptop.
Ask it which concerns scientists raise most, and it counts.
Plain vector search got none of seventeen counting and comparison questions right.
The graph got thirteen.
But the part worth watching is how often my own checks were wrong, and how I found out.
Here is the whole story, with the numbers.
The data is five hundred interviews from the Anthropic Interviewer dataset, where people describe how they use AI at work.
A local model reads each transcript and pulls out tasks, uses of AI, and concerns, each with a quote.
A second small model checks that every quote really supports its claim.
Similar names are merged, and everything goes into Neo4j.
When you ask a question, a router picks one of a few fixed queries.
No model writes database code.
One important limit: the interviews were run by an AI and the people chose to take part, so every count describes this sample, not workers in general.
Here is why a graph.
Ask for the top concerns among scientists, and the answer is a ranked list with counts out of one hundred twenty-five interviews.
Plain retrieval can only show you a few similar answers, so it cannot count.
On my forty test questions, it got zero of seventeen count and comparison questions right.
The graph answered thirteen.
That is the one place the extra machinery clearly earns its place.
How good is the extraction?
I asked a bigger model to check ninety of the extracted facts.
Seventy-eight percent were correct, and ninety percent if you count things the person only wished for.
Concerns were the weak spot, at sixty-three percent.
And recall was worse.
On ten transcripts, the graph captured only about a third of what people actually said.
So counts here are lower bounds.
So I tried to fix recall with a looser prompt for concerns.
Coverage went up, but when I checked a random sample of the new facts, only forty-nine percent were correct and a third were wrong.
I raised the verification threshold, kept about forty percent of them, and tested on a fresh sample so I wasn't grading my own homework.
Seventy-six percent were correct.
Concern coverage on those ten transcripts went from twenty-two to forty-two percent.
A small decision model routes each question.
It picked the right route on thirty-four of thirty-six questions, against thirty-one for a model choosing tools itself.
Shorter route descriptions were faster but it gave up more often, so I kept the longer ones and accepted about two seconds for routing.
On forty questions written by a different model, accuracy was about seventy-five percent, so treat it as good, not perfect.
A language model writing the answer can invent a quote.
So the server builds the facts itself, lets the model only phrase them, and checks every quote and number against the tool output.
If anything doesn't match, it falls back to the plain facts.
Across sixty questions, every delivered quote was real: ninety-eight of ninety-eight.
The price is that about one answer in eight falls back to the plain text.
Then I let a small local model use the tool in ollmcp.
In a long conversation it sometimes skipped the tool and wrote quotes with made-up interview ids.
That happened in three of five runs.
With thinking switched off and the conversation cleared before each question, it relayed the answers faithfully in both runs.
The server cannot force that.
The lesson is that free chat with a small model is unvalidated, so keep the validated path for anything you publish.
Five things I would keep.
One, a graph is worth it for counting and comparing, not for everything.
Two, test any fix on a fresh sample.
Three, say who judged your numbers; mine were a larger model, confirmed by me.
Four, check what a model hands you against the source, every time.
And five, say how much of the data you used.
This was five hundred of twelve hundred fifty interviews.
The code and every result are on GitHub, linked below.
